name: Avinashiappar Temple, Avinashi
deity: Shiva as Avinashiappar (Avinasilingeswarar), with the goddess Karunambikai
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Kongu country, sung in the Tevaram (8th century); structural temple with medieval and later additions
dynasty: Medieval Tamil patrons (Kongu Chola and later)
summary: Avinashiappar is the foremost Shiva temple of the Kongu country praised in the Tevaram, the Thiruppukkoliyur of the hymns, remembered above all for Sundarar's miracle of the child drawn back from the crocodile's mouth.

sections.history: Avinashi, in the Kongu country west of the Kaveri plains, is among the oldest living shrines of the region. In the Tevaram hymns the town is called Thiruppukkoliyur, and tradition honours it as the foremost of the Kongu Nadu temples sung by the saints, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam. Its fame rests above all on the saint Sundarar, who is said to have passed through on his way to Thiruvanchikulam and, by the power of his hymn, to have drawn a long-lost child back from the waters. The name Avinashi is read as the imperishable, and the shrine has carried that sense of permanence across the centuries, raised and enlarged in stone by the medieval patrons of the Tamil country and kept in worship ever since.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east beneath a seven-tiered rajagopuram that rises close to a hundred feet above the Kongu plain. Before it stands a tall lamp-pillar, a deepasthambam carved from a single stone, a feature unusual among the temples of this region. Within the roughly one-and-a-half-acre enclosure the sanctum of Avinashiappar holds the Shiva linga, while the goddess Karunambikai, the mother of compassion, is honoured in her own east-facing shrine beneath a five-tiered gopuram. On the bank of the temple tank stands a shrine to Sundarar, and the base of the flagstaff carries in relief the scene for which the temple is best loved.
sections.legends: The great legend of Avinashi is Sundarar's. Passing through the town, the saint heard from one house the sounds of a wedding and from another the weeping of a household in grief. He learned that two boys had once gone to bathe in the temple tank, and that a crocodile had seized one of them; the family of the lost boy mourned while the other was being married. Moved, Sundarar stood at the water's edge and sang a decad of verses to Avinashiappar. As the hymn reached its fourth verse the crocodile rose and gave up the child unharmed, grown to the age he would have been, and the two boys were wed together. From this the temple keeps the memory of a Lord who makes whole what was lost, and the tank with the saint's shrine beside it is honoured to this day.
sections.festivals: The temple's signature festival is the Mudalai Vaai Pillai Utsavam, the child from the crocodile's mouth, held at Panguni Uthiram in March or April, when Sundarar's miracle is recalled with great feeling. The Chithirai car festival draws the deities out in procession through the town, and the procession of the sixty-three Nayanmar saints is kept with devotion. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Avinashi rewards an unhurried visit. Enter beneath the tall eastern gopuram, pause before the single-stone lamp-pillar, and come to the sanctum of Avinashiappar before turning to the compassionate goddess Karunambikai in her own shrine. Many devotees walk to the temple tank and the shrine of Sundarar on its bank, where the story of the restored child feels close at hand, and families who come to pray for their children hold the place especially dear. The town sits on the busy Coimbatore road, but within the walls the temple keeps the quiet of a very old sanctuary.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Avinashi stands on the Coimbatore–Tiruppur–Erode road, about 13 km from Tiruppur, which is the nearest railway station. Coimbatore, with the region's international airport, is around 35 km away. Frequent buses serve the town, and the temple is at its centre, a short walk from the bus stand.
